--- title: "Federated analysis on GiBleed" subtitle: "A larger, boolean-only OMOP dataset — does a prior peptic ulcer raise the odds of GI bleeding?" format: html: df-print: kable execute: warning: false message: false error: true --- Download the R script (.R) Source (.Rmd) # Welcome In the [first tutorial](dsomop.html) you learned the whole dsOMOP workflow on **MIMIC** (~100 ICU patients). Here we take **exactly the same tools** to a second, **larger** dataset — **GiBleed** (~2,700 patients) — for a more powerful study, and reproduce a classic federated finding: > **Does a prior history of peptic ulcer raise the odds of a gastrointestinal (GI) bleed?** ::: {.callout-important} ## What's different about GiBleed GiBleed is a synthetic OHDSI cohort with **no numeric lab/vital values** — `measurement.value_as_number` is essentially empty. So there is nothing to take a mean or histogram of. Instead, every clinical variable becomes a **boolean** ("does this patient *have* this condition / drug, yes or no?") or a **count** ("how many records?"). Same recipe machinery, different `format`. ::: # 1. Connect ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(DSI); library(DSOpal); library(dsBaseClient); library(dsOMOPClient) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} builder <- DSI::newDSLoginBuilder() builder$append(server = "nairobi", url = "https://nairobi.datashield.live", user = "ethiopia", password = "P@ssw0rd", profile = "omop") builder$append(server = "douala", url = "https://douala.datashield.live", user = "ethiopia", password = "P@ssw0rd", profile = "omop") builder$append(server = "dakar", url = "https://dakar.datashield.live", user = "ethiopia", password = "P@ssw0rd", profile = "omop") conns <- DSI::datashield.login(logins = builder$build()) ds.omop.connect(resource = "omop_demo.gibleed", symbol = "omop", conns = conns) ``` ::: Note the resource is now `omop_demo.gibleed` (not `mimic`). # 2. Confirm there are no numeric values Before choosing how to model, **check the data**. Ask for a numeric summary of any measurement — it comes back empty, which is *why* we will treat everything as boolean: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ds.omop.column.stats("measurement", "value_as_number", scope = "pooled", symbol = "omop", conns = conns)$pooled ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> $n_total #> [1] 44045 #> #> $mean #> NULL ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note} An `NA` mean / zero distinct values confirms `value_as_number` carries no data here. GiBleed records *that* an event happened, not a measured quantity — so our variables will be **presence flags** and **counts**, never means. ::: # 3. The population GiBleed is bigger than MIMIC. Sex, pooled across the three sites: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ds.omop.concept.prevalence("person", concept_col = "gender_concept_id", scope = "pooled", symbol = "omop", conns = conns)$pooled ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| concept_id| n_persons|concept_name | |----------:|---------:|:------------| | 8532| 1370|FEMALE | | 8507| 1315|MALE |
::: ::: ::: {.callout-note} ## A reference year for age GiBleed is a **frozen ~2019 Synthea snapshot**, so we anchor age to **2019** (`omop_variable_age(year = 2019)`) — the dataset's own era, not "today". (For MIMIC we used 2024; each dataset gets its own collection year.) ::: # 4. Explore what was recorded No numbers to plot — so our "distribution picture" is a **prevalence bar chart**: how many patients have each of the most common conditions. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cond <- ds.omop.concept.prevalence("condition_occurrence", metric = "persons", top_n = 12, scope = "pooled", symbol = "omop", conns = conns)$pooled cond <- cond[order(cond$n_persons), ] par(mar = c(4, 17, 2, 1)) barplot(cond$n_persons, names.arg = cond$concept_name, horiz = TRUE, las = 1, col = "#4C72B0", border = NA, xlab = "patients", main = "Most common conditions in GiBleed") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](gibleed_files/figure-html/cond-prev-1.png){width=768} ::: ::: The two variables for our question are in there. **Look them up** to confirm their codes and how many patients they touch: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ds.omop.concept.lookup(c(192671, 4027663), symbol = "omop", conns = conns)$pooled ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| concept_id|concept_name |domain_id |vocabulary_id |standard_concept | |----------:|:---------------------------|:---------|:-------------|:----------------| | 192671|Gastrointestinal hemorrhage |Condition |SNOMED |S | | 4027663|Peptic ulcer |Condition |SNOMED |S |
::: ```{.r .cell-code} cond[cond$concept_id %in% c(192671, 4027663), ] ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| | concept_id| n_persons|concept_name | |:--|----------:|---------:|:------------| |11 | 4027663| 795|Peptic ulcer |
::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip} ## What we're after - **GI hemorrhage** (`192671`) — our outcome. - **Peptic ulcer** (`4027663`) — the antecedent condition we think raises the risk. Both affect enough patients (hundreds each) to model. Notice the long list of near-universal Synthea complaints (osteoarthritis, sinusitis…) — we'll meet one of those again in Section 7. ::: # 5. Build the analysis table (all boolean) A wide person-level table with **sex**, **age** (anchored to 2019), and two **boolean** flags — GI bleed and peptic ulcer: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rec <- omop_recipe( variables = list( omop_variable(table = "person", column = "gender_concept_id", format = "sex_mf", name = "sex"), omop_variable_age(name = "age", year = 2019), omop_variable(table = "condition_occurrence", concept_id = 192671, format = "binary", name = "gi_bleed"), omop_variable(table = "condition_occurrence", concept_id = 4027663, format = "binary", name = "peptic_ulcer") ), output = omop_output(name = "study", type = "wide") ) recipe_execute(rec, out = c(study = "M"), symbol = "omop", conns = conns) ``` ::: **Ratify what the server built**, then read off each flag's prevalence with a frequency table: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ds.colnames("M", datasources = conns) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> $nairobi #> [1] "person_id" "gi_bleed" "peptic_ulcer" "sex" "age" #> #> $douala #> [1] "person_id" "gi_bleed" "peptic_ulcer" "sex" "age" #> #> $dakar #> [1] "person_id" "gi_bleed" "peptic_ulcer" "sex" "age" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} ds.dim("M", datasources = conns) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> $`dimensions of M in nairobi` #> [1] 889 5 #> #> $`dimensions of M in douala` #> [1] 878 5 #> #> $`dimensions of M in dakar` #> [1] 927 5 #> #> $`dimensions of M in combined studies` #> [1] 2694 5 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} as.data.frame(ds.table("M$gi_bleed", datasources = conns)$output.list[["TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts"]]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> #> Data in all studies were valid #> #> Study 1 : No errors reported from this study #> Study 2 : No errors reported from this study #> Study 3 : No errors reported from this study ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display}
| | ds.table("M$gi_bleed", datasources = conns)$output.list[["TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts"]]| |:--|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------:| |0 | 2215| |1 | 479| |NA | 0|
::: ```{.r .cell-code} as.data.frame(ds.table("M$peptic_ulcer", datasources = conns)$output.list[["TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts"]]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> #> Data in all studies were valid #> #> Study 1 : No errors reported from this study #> Study 2 : No errors reported from this study #> Study 3 : No errors reported from this study ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display}
| | ds.table("M$peptic_ulcer", datasources = conns)$output.list[["TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts"]]| |:--|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------:| |0 | 1892| |1 | 802| |NA | 0|
::: ::: # 6. The model Now the question, as a logistic regression across all three hospitals: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fit <- ds.glm( formula = "M$gi_bleed ~ M$age + M$sex + M$peptic_ulcer", family = "binomial", datasources = conns) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} co <- fit$coefficients data.frame( term = rownames(co), OR = round(co[, "P_OR"], 3), CI_low = round(co[, "low0.95CI.P_OR"], 3), CI_high = round(co[, "high0.95CI.P_OR"], 3), p_value = signif(co[, "p-value"], 3), row.names = NULL ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|term | OR| CI_low| CI_high| p_value| |:--------------|-----:|------:|-------:|-------:| |(Intercept) | 0.106| 0.072| 0.154| 0.000| |M$age | 1.001| 0.995| 1.007| 0.736| |M$sexM | 1.006| 0.819| 1.234| 0.957| |M$peptic_ulcer | 3.910| 3.186| 4.799| 0.000|
::: ::: ::: {.callout-important} ## The result A prior **peptic ulcer** multiplies the odds of GI bleeding roughly **four-fold** (OR ≈ 3.9, 95% CI well above 1, p astronomically small) — a strong, clinically coherent signal. **Age** and **sex** are not associated here. With ~2,700 patients the confidence interval is tight: this is the power a larger cohort buys you, and it was produced **without any patient record leaving its hospital**. ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Optional: reproduce the full published model The reference study also adjusts for NSAID drugs. dsOMOP can build a **count across several drug concepts in one variable** — `omop_variable(table = "drug_exposure", concept_id = c(19059056, 1118084, 19078461, 1115171, 1124300), format = "count", name = "nsaid_n")` (aspirin, celecoxib, ibuprofen, naproxen, diclofenac) — and a single-drug flag, e.g. `diclofenac` (`1124300`, `format = "binary"`). Adding them (`gi_bleed ~ age + sex + peptic_ulcer + diclofenac + nsaid_n`) leaves **peptic ulcer dominant**; the drug terms are weak/noise in this synthetic cohort, so don't over-interpret them. ::: # 7. A cautionary tale: when a model breaks Not every variable can be modelled. **Osteoarthritis** (`80180`) is recorded for **every single patient** in GiBleed. Try to predict it: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rec_oa <- omop_recipe( variables = list( omop_variable(table = "person", column = "gender_concept_id", format = "sex_mf", name = "sex"), omop_variable_age(name = "age", year = 2019), omop_variable(table = "condition_occurrence", concept_id = 80180, format = "binary", name = "osteoarthritis") ), output = omop_output(name = "study", type = "wide")) recipe_execute(rec_oa, out = c(study = "OA"), symbol = "omop", conns = conns) fit_oa <- ds.glm("OA$osteoarthritis ~ OA$age + OA$sex", family = "binomial", datasources = conns) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` #> Warning in ds.glm("OA$osteoarthritis ~ OA$age + OA$sex", family = "binomial", : #> Did not converge after 20 iterations. Increase maxit parameter as necessary. ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} fit_oa$coefficients[, c("Estimate", "p-value")] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> NULL ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-important} ## Perfect separation Because the outcome is **100% prevalent** (no "no" group to contrast against), the logistic regression **cannot converge** — you'll see a *"did not converge"* warning and a wildly inflated intercept. The lesson: **always check an outcome's prevalence before modelling it.** A variable everyone (or no one) has carries no information to fit. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} DSI::datashield.logout(conns) ``` ::: --- # Where to go next You have now run the full federated workflow on **two** datasets — numeric-rich MIMIC and boolean-only GiBleed — and seen both a strong result and a broken one. ::: {.callout-note} ## Practise it The **[GiBleed exercise sheet](gibleed-exercises.html)** asks you to find a *different* significant association in this cohort (with hints and a worked, executed [solution](gibleed_solution.html)). :::
